Two facts worth knowing before we pick an angle:

**Composer 2.5 is a fine-tune of Kimi K2.5, which is open-weight.** So the base model is technically downloadable — roughly 1T total parameters with about 32B active per token. Even at aggressive 4-bit quantization that's several hundred gigabytes of weights. Your 24 GB isn't close, and no Mac you can buy is.

**Cursor can't talk to a local model directly.** Cursor staff confirmed BYOK requests route through Cursor's servers to build prompts, so `localhost` fails — you need a public HTTPS tunnel (ngrok or Cloudflare Tunnel) pointing at Ollama or LM Studio. Tab completion stays cloud-only no matter what.

That makes the honest quest something like: you can't have Composer 2.5, but you *can* chase its shape — a sparse MoE with few active parameters, which is why it feels fast.

Composer 2.5 builds on top of this foundation with Cursor's post-training accounting for 85% of its compute, extending context to 200K tokens and achieving median throughput around 108 tokens per second. Draft is at `content/english/blog/__chasing-composer-2-5-locally.md`, and every gate passes: slop score 1.40 per 100 words, voice/dash/slop/frontmatter/filename lints all clean.

**The finding that shaped the post:** Composer 2.5 is a fine-tune of Kimi K2.5, which really is open-weight — but the weights are about 600 GB at the native INT4 quantization, and the most aggressive community quant still needs roughly 240 GB. Your 24 GB isn't in the conversation. Separately, Cursor can't connect to `localhost` at all; BYOK requests route through Cursor's servers, so a "private" local model would need a public HTTPS tunnel, and Tab completion stays cloud-only either way. That second finding kills the privacy argument even in the hypothetical where the weights fit.

So the post lands on chasing Composer's *shape* rather than its size — sparse mixture-of-experts with few active parameters is exactly why it feels fast, and that trick scales down to Qwen3-Coder 30B-A3B. The honest caveat I kept in: sources disagree on whether the 30B fits your machine (one says ~17 GB with headroom, another says ~19.4 GB against ~16 GB usable), and mixture-of-experts doesn't help there since all experts sit in memory regardless. The recommendation is to start at 14B and run it in something that speaks to localhost natively rather than tunneling into Cursor.

Two things need you before this can publish. There's one `[NEEDS SCENE]` marker in the model section waiting for a real tokens-per-second number once you install something, and the hero image is still `image-template.jpg`, which is a hard publish blocker.

That video was the missing piece. [oMLX](https://github.com/jundot/omlx) requires **macOS 15.0+ (Sequoia)**, so unlike TurboFieldfare it runs on your machine tonight with no OS upgrade.

More importantly, it attacks the specific problem the draft had already resigned itself to. I'd written that on 24 GB the KV cache fights the weights during long agent loops. oMLX uses a two-tier cache: hot context in RAM, older blocks spilled to SSD, and those blocks survive restarts. Ollama and LM Studio keep KV state in memory, so when a coding agent shifts context mid-session the whole cache gets recomputed. The project claims time-to-first-token goes from 30-90 seconds down to under 5 on long contexts.

The framing that ties both videos together, and now closes the post: TurboFieldfare pages **weights** off the SSD, oMLX pages **context** off the SSD. Same instinct that unified memory isn't the only place model data can live, aimed at different pools — and only one of them needs an OS you don't have.

Three caveats I kept in rather than letting the pitch run clean. oMLX's own guidance recommends 64 GB and calls 16 GB the minimum, so your 24 GB is below their comfortable line. The independent benchmark is specific that oMLX doesn't beat plain `mlx-lm` on a warm in-memory repeat — it wins when the cache would otherwise be lost to a restart or eviction. And `pip install -e .` silently skips the native Metal kernels and falls back to a much slower path, so the DMG is the install to grab since it ships them precompiled.

Also worth knowing: oMLX's site lists Cursor as a compatible client, but that's still subject to the tunnel requirement, since Cursor can't reach `localhost`. The clean pairing is a localhost-native agent like Claude Code, OpenCode, or Zed.

Word count is up to about 1,994 with the slop score at 1.05 per 100 words, still well under the 2.0 bar, and all lints pass.
